name: Wilks
seoDesc: Wilks: work out wilks coeff. (men) from your body weight and the wilks coeff.. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply your body weight and the wilks coeff. and the Wilks calculator solves for wilks coeff. (men). Think of it as a shortcut for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Wilks calculator work?
sections.html:
The Wilks calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports wilks coeff. (men) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in your body weight and the wilks coeff. (women).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A plain number with no unit attached.

sections.title: The formula behind the Wilks calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Wilks coeff. (men)=-50000000000000 × weight lifted ÷ (1291 × (your body weight ^ 5) − 701863 × (your body weight ^ 4) + 113732000 × (your body weight ^ 3) + 238864500 × (your body weight ^ 2) − 1626063390000 × your body weight + 21604751440000)
Weight lifted=(1 ÷ 50000000000000) × wilks coeff. (women) × (-9054 × (your body weight ^ 5) + 4731582 × (your body weight ^ 4) − 930733913 × (your body weight ^ 3) + 82112226871 × (your body weight ^ 2) − 2723842536447 × your body weight + 59431747775582)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Your body weight = 10 kg and Weight lifted = 10 kg. Working through the relationship above gives Wilks coeff. (women) = 12.6518 and Wilks coeff. (men) = -91.3268.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Wilks coeff. (women) = 12.6518 and Wilks coeff. (men) = -91.3268 should be roughly the size you expected from Your body weight = 10 kg and Weight lifted = 10 kg.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in kilograms, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Wilks calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — your body weight and the wilks coeff. — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Wilks calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Wilks calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns wilks coeff. (men), derived from your body weight and the wilks coeff.. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Wilks calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for your body weight and the wilks coeff., which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter your body weight in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Your body weight opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Wilks coeff. (women) = 12.6518. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Wilks calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
